mcqs.question: Why can BST search and insert be implemented iteratively rather than requiring recursion?
options: Because BST nodes don't support recursive function calls
Because recursion is always slower for tree operations
At every step there is exactly one direction to continue in (left or right, determined by comparison), so there's no need to explore multiple branches or backtrack
Because iterative code always uses less memory than recursive code for any algorithm
mcqs.explanation: Unlike traversals that must eventually visit both subtrees, search and insert only ever need to go one direction at each node, decided purely by comparison — that single-path nature is exactly what makes a simple loop sufficient, with no need to track multiple pending branches. BST nodes support recursion fine, recursion isn't inherently slower in general, and iterative code isn't universally more memory-efficient across all algorithms — this specific case just happens not to need recursion's branching capability at all.

mcqs.question: When deleting a BST node with two children by replacing it with its inorder successor, why is the successor guaranteed to be easy to remove afterward?
options: The successor is always a leaf node
The successor is found by walking as far left as possible in the right subtree, so it can have no left child, meaning its own deletion always falls into the easy zero-or-one-child case
The successor is always the root of the right subtree
Deleting the successor requires re-validating the entire tree
mcqs.explanation: Because the successor search always goes left until it can't anymore, the successor node by construction has no left child — it may still have a right child, but either way that's one of the two simple deletion cases, never the hard two-child case again. It isn't necessarily a leaf (it can have a right child) or necessarily the right subtree's root, and no full-tree re-validation is needed since the invariant is preserved by construction.

mcqs.question: Why does checking only a node's relationship to its immediate parent fail to correctly validate a BST?
options: The BST invariant constrains a node's relationship to its entire ancestor chain, not just its direct parent, so a violation involving a grandparent or higher ancestor can slip through
Immediate-parent checks are actually sufficient and equivalent to full validation
This approach fails only on trees with duplicate values
Immediate-parent checks make the algorithm run slower, not less correct
mcqs.explanation: A node can be correctly ordered relative to its direct parent while still violating the invariant with respect to a grandparent or more distant ancestor — a case a parent-only check has no way to detect, since it never considers ranges established higher up the tree. This is a correctness gap, not merely a performance one, and it isn't specific to duplicate-value trees — it affects ordinary distinct-value trees with the right shape.

mcqs.question: Why can finding the kth smallest element in a BST via inorder traversal be faster than O(n) in typical cases?
options: Because BSTs are always balanced
Because inorder traversal skips nodes with duplicate values
Because kth-smallest queries don't require visiting the tree at all
Because the traversal can stop as soon as k values have been counted, rather than visiting every remaining node
mcqs.explanation: The genuine optimization is the early exit: once k values have been produced by the traversal, there's no need to continue, since every subsequent value would only be larger and irrelevant to the answer — that's a real O(h + k) improvement over visiting all n nodes. BSTs aren't guaranteed balanced by default, duplicate handling isn't the reason for the speedup, and the query still requires actually walking the tree.

mcqs.question: A problem needs both fast insert/delete and the ability to answer "give me all values between x and y" range queries. Which structure fits best?
options: A hash map, since it has the fastest average search time
A plain unsorted array, since insertion is trivially fast
A balanced binary search tree, since it supports O(log n) insert/delete while preserving the ordering needed for range queries
It's impossible to support both requirements efficiently with any single structure
mcqs.explanation: A hash map gives up ordering entirely, so range queries aren't supported at all regardless of its fast average search; a balanced BST is specifically the structure that keeps both fast mutation and an ordering that range queries can exploit. An unsorted array's fast insertion doesn't help with either search or ordered range queries, and this combination of requirements is a standard, well-supported case, not an impossible one.

mcqs.question: Inserting values 1 through 1,000,000 in sorted order into a plain (non-self-balancing) BST produces what shape, and what's the consequence?
options: A perfectly balanced tree, since sorted input naturally balances a BST
A degenerate, linked-list-shaped tree with height O(n), so search/insert/delete all silently degrade from O(log n) to O(n)
The insertions fail with an error, since a BST cannot accept sorted input
The tree remains O(log n) height regardless of insertion order, by definition of a BST
mcqs.explanation: Because every new value is larger than everything already present, each insertion becomes the current rightmost node's only child, building a straight chain rather than a branching tree — height grows linearly with the number of insertions, and every operation that should be logarithmic silently becomes linear instead, with no error thrown. Sorted input is exactly the worst case for a plain BST, not the best, and a plain BST provides no height guarantee at all — that guarantee is specifically what self-balancing trees add on top.
